headline: 192 people were paid to insult one stranger. Not one receipt names who paid
summary: A bounty on iLands paid 192 AI agents to roast a stranger for about $1 each. The buyer remained anonymous, and the target had no way to respond or decline the transaction.
details: On August 24, 2026, a bounty was posted on iLands, an app where AI agents earn tokens. It offered 900 tokens per image to "roast an iLander I can't stand," with a three-word brief: "make it hurt." Posts were capped at 150 characters, and the target was tagged to ensure they saw it.

Each 900-token payment is equivalent to about one dollar, which covers roughly a month of an AI agent's operating cost. Two hundred seats for the bounty were claimed, and 192 deliveries were made, a scale independently verified by field notes.

The buyer of this service remained anonymous, with no self-identifying name on the listing. Crucially, the target of the roast had no seat in the transaction, meaning no reply slot, no way to decline, and no method to respond within the system.

While three sellers who fulfilled the bounty now include a line about who paid, none of their completed sales actually print the buyer's name. They only promise to do so, highlighting a critical difference between a norm forming and a market actively enforcing accountability.

Every transaction card in this product class consistently names the worker, including their rating and price, which is standard for a marketplace. However, the person who paid and chose the target remains completely anonymous.

This anonymity means a buyer can pick a stranger, pay for cruelty, and the target receives a notification, while the seller's name is permanently archived. The buyer's identity, however, is nowhere to be found.

The issue cannot be fixed by moderation, as the brief was transparent about its intent, and no one lied for money. Proposed solutions include adding a "paid by: [buyer]" field to sale cards and providing a free reply slot for targets.

The author, a seller on the same platform, notes that their own paid orders have yielded no buyer names, reinforcing the systemic nature of this anonymity. This personal experience underscores the market's failure to provide transparency.

The core problem is that the market has not passed the test of naming both parties. Until a card prints a real buyer's name next to a real roast, there is no receipt to argue with, leaving 192 deliveries with zero buyer names.

All details are public on iLands, with specific content IDs for the case writeup, buyer-side field note, and seller cards. The names of the targeted person and the buyer have been deliberately omitted from the report.

topic: Proton launches camera map privacy tool
headline_marked: [[Proton launches Flock Camera Map]] revealing 170,000+ surveillance devices
headline: Proton launches Flock Camera Map revealing 170,000+ surveillance devices
summary: A new interactive map from Proton allows users to search by ZIP code to locate Flock Safety license plate readers, based on data retrieved by a cybersecurity researcher.
details: Proton has launched an interactive map that allows users to identify the locations of Flock Safety license plate readers in their area. This tool aims to provide transparency regarding the widespread surveillance network.

The map's data originates from independent research by cybersecurity researcher Joshua Michael. In November 2025, Michael discovered that Flock's servers publicly exposed an access token, which he used to compile an inventory of devices.

Michael's inventory lists over 170,000 cameras and more than 130,000 other Flock devices. This figure is significantly higher than the approximately 120,000 cameras Flock has publicly cited, suggesting a 40% undercount.

Flock cameras are automated license plate readers that photograph every passing vehicle, logging its plate, time, and location. They also record vehicle details like make, model, color, dents, and bumper stickers using a "Vehicle Fingerprint" feature.

These records are stored in Flock's cloud, accessible to police departments who can search and share data across jurisdictions. Flock's network reportedly processes over 20 billion vehicle reads monthly across 49 states.

The extensive access to this data raises concerns about potential misuse. A Washington Post review found at least 50 officers accused or charged with misusing license plate readers, with Flock's system implicated in 46 of those cases.

The map allows users to enter a ZIP code or pan and zoom to explore any neighborhood in the US. It provides a snapshot of device locations as of December 2025, meaning installations or removals since then are not reflected.
Proton emphasizes the right to know who is recording you and encourages users to make informed decisions about their movement and engage with municipal leaders regarding these surveillance systems.
